preamble: Rounding of the close-mid front vowel [e] to [ø] without a change of tongue position. Between Middle High German and modern German, short /e/ was rounded next to labials, /ʃ/ and /l/; the rounded vowel is written ö, and Middle High German already has zwölf beside zwelf. Where the syllable was open, later lengthening gave long /øː/ (schwören, gewöhnen); in closed syllables the vowel stayed short (zwölf, Hölle, Löffel, schöpfen) and is now pronounced [œ]. The same rounding turned i into ü (fünf, Würde).

examples.from: Middle High German swern 'to swear' (Old High German swerien)
examples.note: Wiktionary (gewöhnen, schöpfen) attributes such ö to rounding of Middle High German /e/ next to /ʃ/, /l/ or labials; the modern vowel is long.
Wiktionary attributes the ö to rounding of MHG /e/ next to labials, possibly reinforced by the related gewohnt and Gewohnheit, which have original o.

examples.from: Middle High German zwelf 'twelve' (Old High German zwelif)
Middle High German schepfen 'to scoop' (Old High German skephen)
examples.note: Wiktionary: the rounding of the vowel was caused by the adjacent consonants, as in zwölf and other words with Middle High German /e/.
